title: Human origins
span: about 3.7 million to 44,000 years ago, South Africa
summary: Some of the most important evidence for human evolution comes from South African caves, from early hominins to the first signs of symbolic thought.
caveat: Dates here come from scientific dating methods with error ranges, and several are still argued over. Stops are in order of age, not of discovery.

stops.title: Little Foot
stops.narration: An almost complete Australopithecus skeleton, nicknamed Little Foot, took about 20 years to excavate from the cave rock. The same caves gave up the skull known as Mrs Ples in 1947.
stops.confidence_note: Its age is disputed: one dating method gives 3.67 million years, others suggest closer to 2.6 million.

stops.title: The Taung Child
stops.narration: A child's skull found at a limestone quarry here in 1924 was named Australopithecus africanus by Raymond Dart. Most scientists doubted him for decades; he was right that Africa was central to human origins.
stops.confidence_note: The age is approximate; the marker shows Taung, near the quarry.

stops.title: Wonderwerk Cave
stops.narration: Burnt bone and plant ash deep inside this cave are among the earliest evidence of controlled fire anywhere.
stops.confidence_note: The age and how deliberate the fire was are still studied.

stops.title: Homo naledi
stops.place: Rising Star cave, Cradle of Humankind
stops.narration: Cavers found more than 1,500 bones of a small-brained human relative deep in a hard-to-reach chamber. Why so many bodies ended up there is hotly debated.
stops.confidence_note: Its age range is well dated; claims that it buried its dead are disputed. The marker is placed approximately.

stops.title: Pinnacle Point
stops.narration: People sheltering in these sea caves ate shellfish and ground red ochre, among the earliest such evidence in the world.

stops.title: Klasies River Caves
stops.narration: Remains here are among the oldest known of anatomically modern humans in southern Africa.
stops.confidence_note: Dates vary between layers of the site.
sources: Singer and Wymer, The Middle Stone Age at Klasies River Mouth in South Africa (1982)

stops.title: Blombos Cave
stops.narration: Pieces of ochre engraved with crosshatched lines, along with shell beads, are among the earliest known signs of symbolic thinking.

stops.title: Border Cave
stops.narration: Tools here, including a poison applicator and digging-stick weights, look like those used by San people in recent times, suggesting very long cultural continuity.
stops.confidence_note: Some researchers question how direct the link is to later San culture.
